Prospect: "While the labor share of the national income was roughly 65 percent during the 20 years following World War II, according to a recent report from the New York Federal Reserve Bank, it then began a steady decline to its current 54 percent."

The author, Harold Meyerson, notes that this coincided with the weakening of unions and concludes that the solution is to make unions stronger: "what will be required will be mass organizing on a scale not seen since the 1930s and ’40s, if not greater than that."

I don't disagree, but I do think he misses an important point. It was not just in the US that wage growth stagnated relative to productivity growth. It occurred throughout the world, especially in Japan in the 1970s and 1980s, Germany in the 2000s, and China over the past three decades. It is therefore hard to attribute stagnant wages in the US solely to the political weakening of American trade unions. Something else must have put downward pressure globally on wage growth relative to productivity growth.

An important clue comes later in the article: "Since the end of the 1970s, virtually all American corporations have done everything they could to weaken their workers’ power to increase their income, while they and their investors enjoyed increases in profits, dividends, and buybacks."

The timing is significant. It was in the early 1970s that the US and the world transitioned to our current form of globalization, in which countries could compete aggressively to expand their shares of global manufacturing by suppressing wage growth relative to productivity growth, while externalizing the resulting weak domestic demand by running persistent trade surpluses.

We live in the world, in other words, that Keynes warned against in 1944. While countries that become more competitive by suppressing wages undermine global growth (because rising wages are what drive global demand) they are nonetheless able to grow faster than otherwise. They do so by offsetting weak domestic demand with large, persistent trade surpluses vis-à-vis countries that are less aggressive in suppressing domestic wages.

In this global trading regime, businesses in the US and elsewhere had two choices. Either they had to suppress wage growth at home or, if they wanted to remain competitive, they had to relocate production to countries in which wages were much lower relative to productivity. The dynamic is brutal. We can already see how rapidly China's share of global manufacturing has expanded at the expense of its trading partners – even as its wages remain among the lowest in the world relative to the productivity of its workers.

That is not just a coincidence. It is how our system of globalization has worked: first with Japan and the Asian Tigers, then with Germany, and now with China and other East Asian economies. All of them "succeeded" in growing rapidly and expanding their shares of global manufacturing precisely because wages, relative to worker productivity, were lower than those of their trading partners.

So what would happen if we strengthened unions in the US and forced up wages without changing the rules of the global trading regime? Wages would probably rise temporarily, but US manufacturers would become even less competitive, and the increased purchasing power of American workers would be directed not toward American producers but toward producers abroad that continued to suppress wages.

In fact, higher American wages would actually increase the rewards accruing to countries seeking to expand their shares of global manufacturing by suppressing wage growth.

I am all in favor of strengthening unions and raising wages. In fact, I think high levels of income inequality are the biggest problem facing both the US and the global economy. But as long as we remain part of a global trading regime that rewards wage suppression and penalizes economies that allow wages to keep pace with productivity growth, higher wages will simply mean more deindustrialization.

That is why Keynes proposed a global trading system at Bretton Woods that penalized countries seeking to grow at the expense of their trading partners by suppressing wages or otherwise distorting their domestic economies. His solution was to make it much harder for countries to externalize their domestic imbalances.

Unfortunately, his proposal was rejected. It is almost certainly time to revive it. This is probably what the EU should be doing, especially now that Germany is no longer among the leading beneficiaries of that system.

FT: "According to economic theory, productivity and real wages should grow in tandem, with the benefits of new technology being shared with the workers who produce the stuff. But in the US, Europe and Japan, pay growth has decoupled from...
https://t.co/TZAhk6canO

Sébastien Jean and Jean-Pierre Landau: "In terms of welfare, European consumers should welcome cheap electric vehicles, batteries, and solar panels that are subsidized directly or indirectly by Chinese workers and taxpayers. But Europeans instead see them as a threat, which is rational from a dynamic perspective. Cheap imports may raise purchasing power today, but they can destroy the industrial base on which tomorrow’s income depends. The transfer is generous in the present, but costly in the future."

Jean and Landau are right, and they represent a real shift in the way the world understands trade, away from the complacent (some would even say condescending) neglect still favored by mainstream economists, to a deeper grasp of how trade imbalances allow countries that exert greater control over their external accounts to export their industrial policies (in reverse) to those of their trade partners with more open external accounts. 

In a world in which some economies exert substantial control over their external accounts, in other words, while other countries don't, if the former decide to implement aggressive industrial policies, not only are they restructuring their own domestic economies, but they are also restructuring the domestic economies of the latter in a such a way as to accommodate their own economic needs.

Jean and Landau add: "A useful complement to this strategy is capital controls. Controls on outflows keep domestic savings at home, while restricting inflows prevents the economy from rebalancing from tradable to non-tradable sectors—the opposite of what the strategy aims to achieve. Capital inflows strengthen the currency, weaken exports, and support consumption. They accelerate domestic absorption before scale and learning are secured, thus impeding the pursuit of comparative advantage."

I agree, and this suggests that rather than encourage capital inflows, economies that want to strengthen their manufacturing and productive sectors and to benefit workers by raising productivity and wages should consider capital controls as a far more effective tool than tariffs. Unfettered financial inflows largely benefit the large banks and owners of movable capital at the expense of manufacturers and workers. They also force the economy to shift out of producing tradable goods (including manufacturing) and into non-tradable goods (real estate and services).

The cascade: why D.C. Circuit affirmance effectively cancels SPS conversion
Affirmance finalizes a single controlling fact: the Net Worth Sweep was a breach of the implied covenant — a bad-faith act by FHFA and Treasury against the holders of these specific instruments. Whatever the opinion’s breadth, the judgment cannot stand without that finding standing.

The SPS liquidation preference is not a separate asset from that finding — it is the breach’s residue. The sweep pulled out cash far exceeding what would have retired the seniors on the original 10% terms; the ~$348B balance exists only because those extractions were labeled dividends rather than redemption. Affirmance converts “the balance is arguably illegitimate” into “the mechanism that built the balance has been adjudicated bad faith, and the adjudication is final.”

Conversion is a new act, not a continuation. Treasury exercising a discretionary contractual power to transform that balance into common equity is a second, independent exercise of good-faith-constrained discretion — taken after the courts have spoken. The first breach was committed in legal fog, defensible for a decade as within HERA’s latitude. A conversion would be committed in daylight, against controlling precedent, with scienter effectively built into the public record.

The claim writes itself and the plaintiffs pre-exist. Same instruments, same doctrine, same courthouse, fresh limitations clock — and per the Delaware Supreme Court, the claims travel with the shares, so every holder at conversion is a plaintiff. The complaint’s core allegation would be: the government harvested, as equity, value a federal appellate court already held it accumulated in bad faith. There is no version of that suit the government looks forward to defending.

The warrants make conversion unnecessary. Treasury’s 79.9% position is clean 2008 consideration — pre-breach, bargained-for, already tested and sustained in court. Cancellation-plus-warrants delivers Treasury the dominant share of the upside with zero new legal exposure. Conversion adds incremental value only by taking the remaining ~20% — and that increment is exactly the piece that triggers the suit.

Why it’s functionally impossible, not just legally risky: an exit has to be executable — underwritten, financed, index-eligible, and priced. No underwriter signs a comfort letter, no anchor investor prices a book, and no index committee admits a share class sitting under an unresolved implied-covenant claim seeking rescission of the very equity being sold, backed by an affirmed federal judgment on identical facts. Conversion doesn’t merely invite litigation; it embeds a live rescission overhang into the security itself, which is fatal to the transaction conversion was supposed to enable. Treasury wouldn’t be choosing between a clean exit and a contested one — it would be choosing between an exit and no exit. That’s why affirmance forecloses conversion without ever mentioning it: it leaves cancellation as the only branch that still functions as a transaction.
